content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Righteousness centrally means right standing before God (justification), dominantly framed as God's righteousness imputed/credited to believers through faith apart from works, together with conformity to God's moral character; ethical conduct, infused transformation, covenant faithfulness, and social justice are recognized secondary senses.","book_summary":"Righteousness is 'right-living': God himself is the definitional standard of right, and for humans righteousness is the doing of His commandments. The book concedes that righteousness is 'given and reckoned by grace, not earned as a debt,' but insists the gift 'never renames wrong-living right' — i.e., the term's referent is conduct measured by God's ways, not a status detachable from conduct.","consensus_core_identification":"A compound core: (1) forensic/relational right standing before God received by faith (primary), and (2) conformity to God's moral standard as its accompanying ethical quality, with imputed status as the dominant sense.","book_core_identification":"Righteousness = right-living: actual conformity of conduct to God's commandments and character, with gracious reckoning acknowledged but subordinated — the ethical sense is the term's core, and status language cannot override conduct.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus admits 'righteousness' as a purely declared/legal status possessed by the believer regardless of present conduct (justification of the ungodly as the term's primary referent). The book reclassifies that status sense as secondary: it accepts gracious reckoning (Rom 4:4-8) but excludes cases where 'righteous' would name someone whose living remains wrong ('the gift never renames wrong-living right'). Conversely, it elevates Deut 6:25 / Ps 119:172 / 1 John 3:7 conduct-cases from a common alternative to the primary extension. The book's own common-view note confirms it is deliberately inverting the consensus priority (right-living as core rather than fruit/evidence).","material_contradiction":"None strictly. The book does not deny imputation or grace-reckoning — it cites Rom 4:4-8 and Phil 3:9 approvingly. It disputes priority and boundary (which sense is the term's center and whether status can exist detached from conduct), not the existence of the consensus referent.","rationale":"The book's core identification — righteousness as ethical conduct conforming to God's commandments and character — is explicitly present in the consensus as a 'common' alternative (ethical/behavioral righteousness; cf. 1 John 3:7, Matt 5:20), so it is not NOVEL. It is not DIVERGENT because the book retains the consensus category (rightness measured by God's standard) and expressly affirms the grace-reckoning mechanism the consensus makes primary; both claims can be true of the same referent. But it is not a mere MATCH: the book materially inverts the consensus hierarchy, making right-living the definition and imputed standing a qualified gift that cannot relabel wrong-living, thereby excluding status-without-conduct cases the dominant Protestant reading admits. That is a real boundary/priority change within the same referent — REFINED.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT: the dominant consensus sense is specifically forensic status apart from works (Rom 4:5 'justifieth the ungodly'), and the book's insistence that the gift 'never renames wrong-living right' arguably contradicts justification of the ungodly at the moment of faith, replacing a legal referent with a behavioral one. However, since the book itself cites and affirms Rom 4:4-8 and Phil 3:9, and its ethical core is a listed common alternative, the disagreement reads as reprioritization and boundary-drawing rather than replacement of the referent.","confidence":"high"}
